metadata.llmContext:
Dupesh Nayak is an AI/ML Engineer with deep hands-on experience building production LLM systems across healthcare, BFSI, banking, and observability platforms. The work below is the context the AI assistant should use when answering questions about his background and capabilities.

## 1. Production LLM Experience
The system I would point to first is the Legal Audit platform I built for a multinational BFSI client in the UAE, which their compliance and legal teams use daily. A user uploads a contract; the system extracts the clauses, sends each analysis request through a multi-provider LLM gateway, and returns a structured risk assessment and obligation mapping. Only high-risk items are pushed to a human reviewer. It has been live for several months and carries the client’s ongoing contract review volume.

I own the model layer end to end: provider integration (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen and on-prem models), the routing logic, the Pydantic output schemas, the evaluation set, the fallback behavior, and the cost and latency monitoring in production. The front-end belongs to a separate application team, so a real part of the job was agreeing a clean contract between the two layers and then holding my side of it stable while I changed models underneath it. The compliance officers defined the risk criteria; my job was turning those into acceptance thresholds the system could actually be measured against.

The same model-layer pattern runs through the other three systems: a medical pipeline where a fine-tuned ASR model feeds a domain LLM that produces SOAP notes and structured reports, a real-time log-severity cascade on Grafana and Loki, and an air-gapped signature-matching system inside an Indian bank. Different domains, same underlying problem: find the cheapest model that is good enough for each request, and make the escalation path reliable enough that being wrong is never silent.

## 2. LLM Providers & Models
Providers and models I have run in production:
• OpenAI: complex legal reasoning and clinical report generation.
• Anthropic (Claude Opus / Sonnet class): high-severity log analysis and multi-clause compliance decisions.
• Google Gemini Flash-Lite: high-throughput severity classification in the log pipeline, where the response is a single token and sheer volume is the whole problem.
• Qwen (open-weight, served on-prem with vLLM): privacy-sensitive and cost-sensitive routes in Legal Audit.
• Local vision models (3B / 12B / 80B): air-gapped signature matching for a major Indian bank.

Everything sits behind LiteLLM as a single control plane, so routing, timeouts, fallbacks, token accounting and logging behave identically whether the backend is a public API or a local vLLM endpoint. That is also what keeps the model lineup cheap to change: adding a candidate is a config entry plus an evaluation run, not a new integration. I have not run Groq or Together in production. My throughput-sensitive work went to Gemini Flash-Lite and to on-prem vLLM instead, which is the same trade-off space, and the gateway design means adding either as a provider is a small change rather than a rewrite.

## 3. Model Selection & Routing
Yes. The most fully instrumented one is the router in the Legal Audit platform, and I have applied the same pattern in three other systems.

Before generation I compute a difficulty score from clause density, the number of nested obligations, token length, and a small set of risk tags produced by a lightweight classifier. Semantic embeddings of the clause text separate routine checks from genuine multi-hop legal reasoning, which is the distinction a length-based heuristic on its own keeps getting wrong. Requests below the threshold go to Qwen or a mid-tier model; anything above it goes to OpenAI or Anthropic.

Borderline requests get a cascade rather than a single decision: the cheap model answers first, a fast verifier checks schema compliance and a confidence heuristic, and only then does the request escalate. In production roughly 70% of documents finish on the cheap path and 30% escalate. The threshold is not fixed. I retune it from production data as the client’s document mix shifts.

Against an always-frontier baseline this holds accuracy at 95.1% versus 96.8% while cutting cost per document by about 57%. The full trade-off figures are in question 5.

For free-form user requests the same shape applies with different signals. I classify task type (code, summarisation, maths, legal analysis, open reasoning), required context length, privacy sensitivity, and the latency budget the caller can tolerate, then route to a tier. Legal Audit is the most heavily measured version, but the classify-then-cascade pattern is the same one I would bring to a general-purpose chat product.

Two variations are worth mentioning because they are not text routing. For signatures I route on geometry: simple strokes go to a 3B vision model, complex geometry to an 80B one. For logs there is no classifier at all, just a pure cascade, with Gemini Flash-Lite returning a severity token on every line and Claude Opus invoked only on high-severity events, with the full trace attached.

## 4. Model Evaluation
I do not trust public leaderboards for this. I build a private evaluation set sampled from real production traffic and weighted towards the edge cases that actually break things, and every candidate is tested with identical prompts, inputs and Pydantic schemas so the comparison is honest.

Accuracy is the percentage of correctly extracted fields, risk tags and obligation classifications against a human-annotated gold set. Hallucination rate is the percentage of responses containing claims the source document does not support, measured by deterministic fact matching plus a small human-reviewed sample, because deterministic matching on its own is too generous. The harness is plain Python: an async runner over the LiteLLM surface that writes a per-model scorecard. I kept it in-house rather than adopting an evaluation framework because the scoring is domain-specific, but it does the same job a framework would, and I would happily swap in a standard one where the metrics are generic.

Results from the Legal Audit set:
• Mid-tier / Qwen-class: accuracy 91.4%, hallucination 3.1%, P95 1.4s, .0042 per document.
• Frontier: accuracy 96.8%, hallucination 1.2%, P95 3.9s, .019 per document.
• Routed hybrid (roughly 70% mid-tier, 30% frontier): accuracy 95.1%, hallucination 1.8%, P95 2.1s, .0081 per document.

I shipped the hybrid because it matched how the client ranked their priorities: accuracy and low hallucination first, cost and latency second. On a product with a different ranking I would have chosen differently, and that ranking is a conversation to have with the business rather than a number to optimise in isolation.

## 5. Quality vs. Cost vs. Speed
The clearest example is Legal Audit before the router existed. Sending everything to a frontier model was roughly 2.3 times more expensive and about twice as slow at P95, and the client had a genuine budget ceiling. Sending everything to a cheap model missed the compliance team’s accuracy bar. Neither single-model answer was acceptable, which is what forced the routing work.

So I split the traffic. The difficulty score and cascade put about 70% of documents on cheaper models and escalated 30%. Average cost per document fell 57%, P95 on the non-escalated majority dropped from 4.8s to 2.1s, and accuracy came in at 95.1% against the frontier’s 96.8%. Trading 1.7 points of accuracy for that cost and latency profile was a decision I made explicitly with the compliance stakeholders and documented, rather than one that quietly emerged from a config change.

The log pipeline is the same trade-off at a different scale. Gemini Flash-Lite classifies every line and returns only a severity token; Claude Opus is called solely on high-severity events, together with the full trace context. That cut expensive-model token volume by more than 80% while keeping the deep reasoning exactly where it earns its cost.

## 6. Python & Engineering
Python is where the entire model layer lives. The production services are FastAPI with Pydantic for strict contracts, LiteLLM for the provider surface, LangChain and LangGraph for multi-step flows, and asyncio throughout for concurrent request handling.

I wrote the full path myself: scoring function, model selection, timeout and retry, fallback, telemetry, and the post-deployment evaluation loop. Around that sit vLLM and TensorRT for local serving, structured logging and containerisation. Outside the request path I also wrote the evaluation harness, the shadow-traffic runner used before promoting a model, and the batch jobs that pull production telemetry back into threshold tuning. I work with the application team on integration points and with the compliance or clinical stakeholders on what counts as an acceptable answer.

## 7. Reliability & Fallbacks
Yes, and the three cases are handled differently because they fail differently:
• Provider unavailable or 5xx: LiteLLM fails over to the next healthy provider, or to the on-prem replica if the outage is provider-wide. Health is tracked per provider, so a route that keeps failing drops out of rotation instead of being retried into.
• Too slow: Hard timeouts, typically 3s on the cheap path and 8 to 12s on the frontier path. On timeout the request is re-routed to a backup model. If that also fails, the caller gets an explicitly marked incomplete response that cannot bypass the human-review path. A late answer is recoverable; a silently wrong one is not.
• Poor response: Pydantic validation rejects malformed output before it reaches anything downstream. The request is then retried on a stronger model or escalated to a human with the original payload preserved, so the reviewer sees exactly what the model saw.

Downstream systems (ERP, core banking, alerting) only accept responses that have passed the schema and completeness checks. In compliance and banking contexts the only safe failure is a visible one, so nothing is allowed to degrade quietly.

## 8. LLM Optimization
The largest single improvement I have measured was on the medical pipeline. I fine-tuned a 24B MoE ASR model with LoRA on domain audio and took domain accuracy from 81% to 94.5%. It belongs in this answer because the transcript is the input to the clinical LLM: fixing drug names and dosages upstream removed a whole class of downstream generation errors that no amount of prompt engineering was going to fix.

Getting there was not clean. I tried Whisper Large v3, Granite, Qwen3, Canary and Wav2Vec2 first, and all five underperformed on domain terminology when I evaluated them against a held-out sample from the client’s own dataset rather than a public benchmark — drug names and dosages were where they broke most often. Voxtral was the first base model accurate enough to be worth fine-tuning, and getting it from there to 94.5% took real iteration: LoRA hyperparameters, system prompts, and the learning-rate schedule all went through several rounds before the client’s sample set passed.

On the prompt and structured-output side I cut average output tokens by about 35% and raised schema compliance from 91% to 99.4%, mostly by tightening the Pydantic models so the schema itself carried the constraints instead of restating them in prose inside the prompt. Shorter output also meant lower latency, so for once the two goals pulled in the same direction.

For local serving I tuned vLLM and TensorRT, including KV-cache and batching settings, so that concurrent users stayed inside the latency targets on fixed on-prem hardware.

The routing and cascade work covered earlier is the other half of this: 57% off cost per document, with P95 down from 4.8s to 2.1s on the majority path.

## 9. Monitoring & Production Data
Per model and per route I track:
• Latency (mean and P95) and throughput.
• Token usage and cost per request and per document.
• Schema-validation failure rate and fallback rate.
• Quality signals from human reviewer feedback and automated checks.
• Escalation volume, and time-to-alert for the log cascade.

Cost and token accounting come out of LiteLLM callbacks into structured logs, and the same Grafana surface I built for the log-severity product serves the model telemetry. The point is not the dashboard. Escalation rate drifting upwards is how I know the difficulty threshold needs retuning; a schema-failure rate rising on one provider and not the others is usually the first sign that something changed on their side rather than mine. Before promoting a new model I run it under shadow traffic against the live router, and a short A/B test when volume allows it.

## 10. Open-Weight Models
Three production settings:
• The Qwen family served on-prem with vLLM for the privacy- and cost-sensitive routes in Legal Audit, chosen because those contracts could not leave the client’s infrastructure.
• Three vision models (3B, 12B, 80B) running fully air-gapped inside a major Indian bank for signature and cheque processing, with no external network path at all.
• A custom 24B MoE ASR model that I fine-tuned with LoRA and containerised for the medical pipeline.

All of them sit behind the same LiteLLM surface as the cloud providers, so routing and observability do not change shape when a request goes local. In practice the three things that decide whether an open-weight model is usable are quantisation level, context length under real concurrency, and serving configuration, and I have had to tune all three against fixed hardware. Most of my hands-on time is with Qwen; I have benchmarked Llama and Gemma against the same private evaluation set but have not run them in production.

## 11. Ownership & Problem-Solving
Legal Audit is the clearest case. The client needed accurate risk tagging at a cost and latency the business could sustain, and both obvious answers failed: a single frontier model broke the budget, a single cheap model missed the compliance bar. I designed and built the difficulty score, the cascade quality gate, the LiteLLM gateway, the Pydantic contracts, the evaluation set and the production telemetry, and I still own the thresholds today.

A practical failure on Legal Audit: the compliance framework for a given clause was often far larger than the contract itself, and sending that full framework to the LLM made token usage and latency balloon while irrelevant requirements sometimes outweighed the relevant ones in the model's reasoning — I caught it when cost-per-document on complex clauses spiked well past the budget the client had signed off on. I replaced 'send everything and let the model sort it out' with a retrieval and reranking step: hybrid lexical plus semantic retrieval narrowed the candidate requirements, a reranker scored them on relevance, risk tag and clause type, and only the top set reached the reasoning model. That cut the context window down to what mattered, brought cost and latency back in line, and made every decision traceable to the specific requirements retrieved.

The bank signature system was a different kind of ownership. The constraint that shaped every decision was that nothing could leave the bank’s network, so there was no cloud option to fall back on and the accuracy and latency targets had to be met on hardware already inside the building. I decomposed signatures into stroke layers, selected and deployed three differently sized open-weight vision models on-prem, implemented the coordinate-aware routing between them, and worked with the bank’s operations team to fit the matcher into the existing cheque-clearance workflow.

## 12. AI Ecosystem
When a model is released I put it through the private benchmark suite I already maintain: the same production-like samples, the same prompts, the same schemas, scored on accuracy, hallucination, P95 and cost. If the numbers look promising it goes under shadow traffic against the live router before it handles anything real. Only if it improves the current trade-off does it get promoted, and if it does not, it stays offline. In a routed system a new model has to earn a specific slot, not just post a good benchmark score.

Most recently that meant evaluating newer Gemini Flash-Lite variants for the high-throughput severity path and Claude Opus 5 for deep log reasoning, scored on exactly the metrics the production cascade optimises. I run the same process for open-weight candidates on the on-prem routes. Day to day I follow provider changelogs and release notes, new model cards as they land on Hugging Face, and independent latency and cost benchmarks rather than launch-day marketing numbers, because the things that decide a routing change (real P95, real cost per token, real schema reliability under load) are almost never in the announcement.

This is the experience and production operating model Dupesh brings to AI engineering work: multi-model routing, cost-aware LLM architecture, rigorous evaluation, reliable fallbacks, and domain-specific optimization under real business constraints.
